items.title: Australian MP Loses Both Legs After Alleged Car Attack
items.summary: A sitting federal MP is at The Alfred after bilateral amputations following a deliberate ramming in Wangaratta.

_homepage.note: Helen Haines, the member for Indi, was struck outside her electorate office on Monday; her left leg was amputated that day and surgeons could not save the right. The pathway is the familiar one — regional retrieval into a Melbourne major trauma service — and it is The Alfred fronting the press conferences. It also lands weeks out from the Victorian election, which is the political weather the state's health system is about to be funded by.

items.title: Beyond Average: New Benchmarks for Paediatric Emergency Care
items.summary: Quality targets pegged to what the best clinicians already achieve, rather than to a national average or an unreachable 100 per cent.

_homepage.note: Alpern's group mined 5.3 million PECARN visits across twelve departments and 925 clinicians to build Achievable Benchmarks of Care, which is a different exercise from the usual audit against a mean. The metrics being benchmarked are the familiar paediatric ones, so this reads naturally alongside the Don't Forget the Bubbles material already in the feed. The method is the transferable part: it is an argument about how any ED target should be set.

items.title: Interview: Mastering Engineer Ryan K. Smith at the Vinyl Summit
items.summary: The lacquer-cutting end of a record, from the Nashville engineer whose name turns up in the run-out grooves of a lot of modern reissues.

_homepage.note: Day two of the Vinyl Summit in Salina, and Smith is one of the few people interviewed who actually cuts the lacquer rather than discussing the finished object. The day-one report is already in the feed, so this carries it from the mastering chain into the physical cut. It is the part of the chain that decides whether a reissue sounds like the tape or like a loud file.

items.title: Nigeria Confirms Imported Ebola Bundibugyo Case
items.summary: The DRC Bundibugyo outbreak has reached a fifth country, this time through a traveller returning from Uganda.

_homepage.note: WHO was counting 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths as of 6 October, a crude case fatality ratio just under half, with Ituri still the worst-affected province. Every export so far — Kenya first, now Nigeria — has been travel-associated, which is the pattern that eventually puts a febrile returned traveller in front of an Australian triage desk. Knowing which countries are on the list is the part that changes a history-taking.

items.title: ACLS Arrhythmia Pitfalls: Unstable Tachycardia, Cardiovert?
items.summary: The case against reflexively shocking a fast, sick patient when the tachycardia is the compensation and not the cause.

_homepage.note: Jesse McLaren's argument is that sinus tachycardia, or AF with rapid ventricular response in a shocked patient, is usually secondary, and cardioverting it treats the monitor instead of the problem. This is the call made at the bedside before anyone senior arrives, and it is the one the ACLS algorithm handles worst. Sits directly alongside the EMCrit piece on RSI in shocked patients already in the feed.

items.title: ACLS Arrhythmia Pitfalls: Stable Wide Complex Tachycardia
items.summary: Regular, genuinely wide complexes at an unremarkable rate point at hyperkalaemia or sodium-channel blockade rather than VT.

_homepage.note: The tell is the mismatch — a very wide QRS without the rate you would expect from ventricular tachycardia should push you toward potassium and toxicology before amiodarone. It is the companion instalment to the unstable-tachycardia piece, and both are built as ECG cases rather than prose. Useful revision for the ECG-interpretation end of fellowship prep, where this exact discrimination gets tested.

items.title: Inside Strata-East, the Artist-Owned Label That Changed Jazz
items.summary: Why the most collectable jazz label of the seventies was the one where the musicians kept their own master tapes.

_homepage.note: Charles Tolliver and Stanley Cowell built it so artists financed their own sessions, held their masters and shared the profits — the opposite of the major-label arrangement, and the reason original pressings are so thin on the ground. The collection already leans into the hard-bop and soul-jazz end through Oscar Peterson, Milt Jackson and Stan Getz, and the Mack Avenue reissue campaign has made Glass Bead Games and Capra Black gettable again. The Bandcamp primer in the feed covers which records to buy; this covers why they exist at all.

items.title: 12 Months, 12 Cameras: The Project That Changed How I Shoot
items.summary: A year spent using the cameras already on the shelf instead of buying the next cheap body.

_homepage.note: Katya Rowny's rule was one camera a month, drawn from what she already owned, which turns an accumulation habit into a deliberate exercise and forces you to learn each body's quirks properly. It reads as a direct counterweight to the gear-acquisition end of film photography, and the structure is simple enough to start in November. Sits well beside the Hasselblad Super Wide and Leica M4 pieces already here, both of which were about committing to one camera at a time.

items.title: Warren Boasts the Heaviest Flannel We've Ever Seen
items.summary: A 16oz shirting flannel woven to order at American Woolen, four ounces past what the Japanese labels call ultra-heavy.

_homepage.note: The cloth is the whole story here: custom-developed with American Woolen in Connecticut, offered in Birch Buffalo, Peat Herringbone and Blue Hour Ombre, with corozo buttons and a hidden button-down collar. That mill-and-pattern territory is the same one the vintage Woolrich and Pendleton reference points occupy, except made now and traceable to a named weaver. At $295 it is priced against the heavy-flannel Japanese labels rather than against a department-store plaid.

items.title: Analog.Cafe Podcast: A Conversation With Sissi Lu
items.summary: The New York street portraitist on consent, scanning, and making a living shooting film full time.

_homepage.note: Lu works by asking — her portraits of strangers, and particularly of older subjects, come out of a conversation rather than a long lens, and she is unusually direct about the ethics of it. The interview also gets practical on scanning and on handling large commercial clients, which is the part most photographer profiles leave out. She is also the person behind the DO NOT X-RAY travel pouch, which is worth knowing about before the next flight with a few rolls in the bag.

items.title: Game Developers Pitch for Funding, Speed-Dating Style
items.summary: The funding bottleneck behind Australia's biggest game development city, staged as a room full of three-minute pitches.

_homepage.note: Melbourne carries most of the country's game development, and this is the mechanism by which its small studios actually find money — publishers and investors in a room, timed rounds, no long decks. Worth reading if you want to know who is building things here rather than only what eventually appears on the PlayStation store. It is the part of Melbourne culture that never surfaces in the dining and exhibition listings.

items.title: AI Upscaling Is Coming to PS5
items.summary: Sony is opening its QSSR upscaler to every PlayStation developer, which quietly changes what the current console can hold.

_homepage.note: This is a platform-level change rather than a game announcement, so the gain arrives across the catalogue instead of in one showcase title. For a large streamed survival world — the Enshrouded and Dragonwilds end of the shelf — reconstruction is exactly where the frame budget goes, and this is the lever that frees it. First-party, dated, and worth reading before the next round of remaster claims.
